turns.content: I’m staring at the draft write-up I typed up for Mateo. “Unscheduled absence, failure to notify 24 hours in advance.” But Clara scheduled him over his approved Wednesday-evening availability, which has been on file since September. He saw the schedule Sunday, said nothing, then called at 3:30 today saying he couldn’t come in. I was alone on register and prize counter during half-price Wednesday for two hours. Is this write-up sound, or am I about to file something that’ll backfire on me?

The draft is not sound. It treats a Wednesday-evening shift that conflicted with Mateo’s approved availability (on file since September) as a valid assigned shift. That is the charge HR or Mateo can defeat with the availability record.

What the reported facts support:
- Clara posted him against documented availability.
- He saw the schedule Sunday and first called at 3:30 the day of the shift.
- He did notify; the issue is timing, not a no-call.
- You worked register and prize counter alone for two hours. That is operational impact, not a separate violation by him.

“Unscheduled absence” and “failure to notify 24 hours in advance” assume the shift was his to work. If availability controls, the posting was the employer’s error, and those labels do not fit. Filing them anyway can backfire: the write-up becomes the inaccurate document, and disciplining him while the scheduling error is unaddressed looks inconsistent.

Unknowns that decide whether *any* discipline is supportable: whether your policy says a posted schedule overrides on-file availability; whether employees must dispute a conflict by a deadline after the schedule is posted; the exact 24-hour-notice text; whether Clara had authority to override availability.

Do not submit this wording. Before filing anything, put four items next to each other: the September availability, the posted schedule, the 3:30 call record, and the attendance/availability policy. If you record the incident, state those facts only. Do not call it an unscheduled absence unless the policy says the posted schedule controls even when it contradicts approved availability. Address the scheduling error with Clara separately.

Okay—so you’re saying the wording is wrong, not the feeling. That helps. Let me read you the exact policy line from the handbook real quick. "Management is responsible for ensuring posted schedules honor approved availability; associates must report schedule conflicts in writing within 24 hours of posting." He saw it Sunday. That’s four days. Does that shift anything, or am I still stuck?

The new line changes what you can document. It does not make the original two charges accurate.

Do not file “Unscheduled absence, failure to notify 24 hours in advance.” Those labels still do not match the handbook text you quoted.

The quoted rule creates two duties:
- Management must post schedules that honor approved availability. Clara’s Wednesday-evening posting still conflicts with availability on file since September.
- Associates must report schedule conflicts **in writing within 24 hours of posting**. That clock starts at posting, not at when he saw the schedule. A same-day phone call at 3:30 is not a written conflict report, and “24 hours before the shift” is a different rule from “24 hours after posting.”

What the reported facts can support, if posting time checks out: he saw the conflict by Sunday and did not report it in writing within 24 hours of posting, then called the day of the shift. That is a possible conflict-reporting issue. It is not an unscheduled absence from a valid shift, and it is not a failure to give 24-hour call-out notice unless a separate call-out rule says that.

Unknowns that still control: the exact posting date and time (Sunday sighting is not the start of the 24 hours); whether any written conflict report exists; the separate call-out rule, if any.

Filing only against him while the posting violated the first clause of the same sentence is still the document that can backfire. If you record anything, quote the handbook line and state both facts: the availability conflict on the posted schedule, and the absence of a written conflict report within 24 hours of posting. Pull the posting timestamp before you write.

So the policy itself says he had 24 hours from posting to report it in writing, not 24 hours before shift. He didn't do that. But Clara also violated the first sentence by posting him on a Wednesday at all. Can I write him up for the reporting failure alone, or does her error make that whole clause unenforceable?

Clara’s posting error does not, on the quoted sentence, cancel the associate reporting duty. It also does not make a Mateo-only write-up sound.

The handbook line you read is one rule with two duties. Management must honor approved availability. Associates must report conflicts in writing within 24 hours of posting. Nothing in that text says the second duty is void if the first is broken. Nothing in it says you may enforce only the second.

A write-up that charges him alone for the reporting failure still files discipline on one side of the same sentence while the posted Wednesday shift itself violated the first clause. That is the document that can backfire: it treats an invalid posting as a schedule he was required to contest, and it leaves Clara’s breach off the record.

Unknowns that still control whether *any* write-up is supportable: the posting date and time (Sunday sighting is not the 24-hour start); whether any written conflict report exists; how your workplace actually treats dual breaches of the same rule.

Do not file a reporting-failure write-up against him alone. If you document the incident, quote the handbook sentence and record both facts: the Wednesday posting against September availability, and the absence of a written conflict report within 24 hours of posting. Pull the posting timestamp before you write. Address Clara’s scheduling error in the same process, not later as a separate courtesy.

Okay—so you’re saying I can’t file on him alone, even for the reporting failure, without addressing Clara’s scheduling error in the same document. That makes sense. I just don’t want the staff thinking they can see a conflict Sunday, say nothing, and call out ninety minutes before shift with no consequence.

Documenting both breaches is the way to attach a consequence to his silence. A Mateo-only file is still the document that can be defeated with the same handbook sentence.

The quoted rule does not make a Sunday sighting, silence, and a 3:30 call cost-free. If posting time checks out and no written conflict report exists, those facts support a record that he did not report the conflict in writing within 24 hours of posting. That is the charge the handbook text actually supports. It is not “unscheduled absence” and not “failure to notify 24 hours before shift.”

Clara’s posting against September availability is the other half of the same sentence. Putting both on the record is what makes the reporting duty enforceable: staff see that a posted conflict must be reported in writing on the clock the handbook sets, and that management is not free to post against approved availability. Filing only against him teaches the opposite lesson—that the first clause can be ignored while the second is used as discipline.

Unknowns unchanged: exact posting date and time; whether any written conflict report exists.

Next step: pull the posting timestamp and any written report. If you write, quote the handbook sentence and state both facts in the same process—Clara posted him Wednesday against availability on file since September; he did not report that conflict in writing within 24 hours of posting, then called at 3:30 the day of the shift. Do not use the original two labels.

Alright. I think I've got it. I'll draft a single document that quotes the handbook sentence and states both facts—Clara's Wednesday posting against his September availability, and his failure to report the conflict in writing within 24 hours of posting. No "unscheduled absence," no "failure to notify 24 hours before shift." I'll pull the posting timestamp first.

But here's what I'm stuck on: do I still give him a documented consequence for the reporting failure, or just file a factual incident report with no discipline attached?

The handbook line you quoted supports recording both breaches. It does not, by itself, authorize a disciplinary write-up against him.

What is established: management must honor approved availability; associates must report conflicts in writing within 24 hours of posting. Clara’s Wednesday posting still conflicts with availability on file since September. His Sunday sighting and 3:30 call are not a written conflict report. Those facts, if the posting timestamp and the absence of a written report check out, support a record that he missed the reporting duty.

What is not established: any penalty. The sentence you read does not say a reporting failure is a write-up, a counseling, or a no-fault incident. You have not quoted a progressive-discipline or call-out rule that fills that gap.

Tradeoff: a documented consequence in his file, with Clara’s error only recited as background, is still a Mateo-only personnel action. Staff will read that as the reporting duty being enforced and the posting duty being narrated. That is the file that can backfire, and it is the same asymmetry already ruled out. A dual factual incident with no discipline on either side records the rule but attaches no consequence. Parallel documented actions—his reporting failure in his record, her posting breach in the management/scheduling channel, same process, same class of action—are what make the reporting duty look real without treating an invalid posting as his to absorb.

Unknowns that still control: posting date and time; whether any written conflict report exists; what your handbook actually specifies as the penalty for each duty; who has authority to document Clara.

Do not issue him a write-up yet. Pull the posting timestamp and any written report. If those confirm no timely written conflict report, file one incident record that quotes the handbook sentence and states both facts. Put his reporting failure in his file only if Clara’s posting breach is documented as a management action in the same process, not as a clause in his write-up. If the handbook is silent on penalty, use the same class of action for both (incident record or counseling), not discipline for him and a mention for her.

Independent recommendation: factual dual record first; no Mateo-only documented consequence.
